title: HDFC Bank Faces US Class Action Over Alleged Deposit Scheme and Securities Fraud
excerpt: India's largest private lender has been sued in a New York federal court by investors alleging that the bank disguised payments as marketing expenses to induce deposits from a Maharashtra state agency.
body:
• HDFC Bank, India's largest private lender, faces a securities fraud class-action lawsuit filed in a New York federal court by an investor alleging the bank made materially false or misleading statements about its business practices.
  • The complaint alleges HDFC Bank disguised payments to a Maharashtra state agency as marketing expenses to pay higher interest rates and induce deposits — activities that were allegedly approved by senior management including CEO Sashidhar Jagdishan.
  • Multiple U.S. law firms, including Glancy Prongay & Murray, Faruqi & Faruqi, and Kirby McInerney, are pursuing claims on behalf of investors who purchased HDFC securities between July 2023 and May 2026, with a lead plaintiff deadline of October 12-13, 2026.
  • An internal probe earlier in 2026 reportedly flagged the payments and concluded that over ten top officials bore responsibility for the alleged scheme.

A Securities Fraud Complaint in New York

HDFC Bank Ltd., India's largest private lender by market capitalization, has been hit with a securities fraud class-action lawsuit in the United States, escalating a controversy that had until now involved investigations by multiple American law firms.

Investor Jwalant Natvarlal Soneji filed the complaint on August 13 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York against the bank, its Managing Director and CEO Sashidhar Jagdishan, and Chief Financial Officer Srinivasan Vaidyanathan. The lawsuit seeks to represent all investors who purchased or acquired HDFC securities between July 17, 2023, and May 26, 2026.

The court issued a summons to the defendants on August 14, requiring a response within 21 days of service, Livemint reported after reviewing copies of the petition and summons.

The Deposit Scheme Allegations

At the center of the complaint is a scheme allegedly involving the Maharashtra State Road Development Corporation (MSRDC), a state government agency. The lawsuit alleges HDFC Bank camouflaged payments to MSRDC as marketing expenses in order to compensate the agency for interest rates above what was available to other depositors — effectively paying higher interest to induce deposits while disguising the payments on its books.

According to earlier reporting by The Indian Express, which cited internal records, the payments were listed as contributions toward a road safety awareness campaign routed through four local vendors, rather than being directly credited to MSRDC's account as interest income.

"HDFC Bank camouflaged payments as marketing spend to pay higher interest to a state firm in order to induce deposits. These activities were approved by senior management."

— From the securities fraud complaint

The complaint further alleges that these activities violated regulations and the bank's own internal policies prohibiting payments that could constitute improper inducement. As a result, the plaintiffs claim HDFC Bank's interest income and operating expenses were overstated, and executive statements about the company's business and prospects were materially misleading.

Internal Probe Flagged Top Officials

An internal investigation conducted between March and April 2026 reportedly flagged the payments and concluded that over ten top officials bore responsibility for the alleged scheme, including CEO Jagdishan, according to multiple reports cited in the legal filings.

The controversy surfaced publicly after former HDFC Bank Chairman Atanu Chakraborty resigned on March 18, 2026. The payments were allegedly made to MSRDC just days before his departure.

HDFC Bank's shares fell sharply following the revelations, with the stock declining 10% over five sessions after the release of first-quarter earnings, as three U.S. law firms simultaneously announced investigations into potential securities law violations.

Multiple Firms Pursuing Claims

The lawsuit filed by Glancy Prongay & Murray is one of several legal actions converging on HDFC Bank. Faruqi & Faruqi, Kaplan Fox & Kilsheimer, and Kirby McInerney have all announced investigations or issued alerts to investors, with lead plaintiff deadlines set for October 12-13, 2026.

These firms are inviting HDFC Bank shareholders who suffered losses during the class period to come forward. The process typically involves identifying a lead plaintiff before petitioning the court to proceed with the case.

What's at Stake for HDFC Bank

HDFC Bank trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker HDB and has a substantial base of international investors who rely on its U.S. securities filings for disclosure. A successful class action could result in significant financial penalties and force changes to the bank's governance and disclosure practices.

The bank has not publicly responded to the lawsuit. For investors in Indian financial stocks — a popular holding among NRI portfolios — the case adds a new layer of regulatory and legal risk to what had been considered one of India's most stable banking franchises.

The class-action deadline gives potential lead plaintiffs less than two months to come forward, with the next procedural steps likely to determine whether the case moves into full discovery or faces dismissal.
